case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court clarified the family court standard of review, holding that while appellate courts review de novo and may find facts by their own view of the preponderance of the evidence, the appellant still bears the burden of showing error and the family court's credibility findings are respected.
key_cases.relevance: Any systematic analysis of reversal rates in South Carolina child welfare appeals must be read against the Lewis de novo-plus-burden framework.
key_cases.quote: consistent with our constitutional authority for de novo review, an appellant is not relieved of his burden to demonstrate error in the family court's findings of fact

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's reasonable-efforts provision, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by beneficiaries under the Act itself or under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
key_cases.relevance: Any cross-chain compliance analysis must account for Suter's rule that most federal child-welfare mandates are conditions on funding, not enforceable rights.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

key_cases.case_name: White Ex Rel. White v. Chambliss
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held South Carolina DSS officials were entitled to qualified immunity on claims arising from the removal of children and the foster placement in which one child died, because no clearly established federal right — including any right created by the South Carolina Child Protection Act — was violated.
key_cases.relevance: Cross-chain analysis of South Carolina must reflect that state statutory violations here generate no federal cause of action under White.
key_cases.quote: The facts presented by White reveal that the DSS defendants violated no "clearly established" law in removing White's children from her custody.

key_cases.case_name: Disabato v. South Carolina Ass'n of School Administrators
key_cases.holding: The court held that applying the South Carolina FOIA to a nonprofit corporation supported in part by public funds does not violate its First Amendment speech and association rights, and reversed dismissal of the FOIA action.
key_cases.relevance: Automated transparency analysis of South Carolina must include publicly funded private entities that Disabato brings within FOIA.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that while the FOIA does impact upon SCASA's speech and association rights, the First Amendment is not violated.
